proposals.title: Derive each lock's pinning from the required-key set before spending any check
proposals.trigger: The observation exposes a deterministic derivation from a key's cut vector to a lock's accepted set (a cut lifts the pin stack, interfaces align at the shear plane), and the access table states, per key, which locks must open and which must stay shut. A check is a costly confirmation of an assignment, not a source of information the derivation does not already contain.
procedure: Fix the key cut vectors first. They are the free variables; every lock's open/reject behaviour is a function of them, so choosing them late forces a rebuild of everything downstream.
For each lock, collect the cut vectors of the keys it must open. That collection is the exact set of bittings its pinning has to accept -- not an approximation to be tuned toward.

Construct that lock's pinning so every required cut vector is admitted and no non-required key is admitted in every chamber. The accepted set is the product of the per-chamber accepted cuts, so extra unassigned bittings are unavoidable once a lock needs three distinct required keys under a two-shear cap; they are an efficiency cost, not a violation.

Before committing, test the whole assignment in your head: if any non-required key's cut vector lies in every chamber's accepted set, that pair is open by construction. Change the assignment, do not plan to patch it after a check.
Derive all locks and all keys to consistency, then issue one check. Treat its report as pass or fail; treat a failure list as a signal that the derivation was wrong, not as a queue of edits.
successSignals: A single check is issued, after the assignment is complete, and it returns no required failures and no forbidden openings.
Violation lists, when they exist at all, shrink between revisions rather than moving to different locks.
A lock's admitted bittings are equal by construction to the set of keys the table requires it to admit.
failureSignals: Checks are issued while the assignment is still being built, and each check is followed by a small local edit to the pairs it named.
Forbidden openings reappear scattered across many different locks after each revision -- the signature of patching one pair by breaking another.
The action budget runs out while the check still reports open forbidden pairs.
recovery: If a check reports forbidden openings, discard the incremental edits and re-derive the affected keys' cut vectors and the affected locks' pinning from the table in one pass.
If the derivation cannot satisfy the table, re-examine which keys share locks: a key required by several locks constrains those locks jointly, so its cut vector must be chosen before theirs.
invariants: Every lock's accepted set is a function of the key cut vectors alone; no world action reveals a pair the derivation cannot already compute.
A key opens a lock only if it is admitted in every chamber, so a single chamber can carry the whole rejection.

proposals.title: Count per-chamber interfaces while choosing master wafers, not after the check
proposals.trigger: While building a lock's pin stack so that a chamber admits more than one required cut, the stack gains bottom-pin/master-wafer interfaces. The per-chamber shear-point maximum is stated in the model at the start, and it bounds how many interfaces that chamber may carry.
procedure: For each chamber of each lock, count the interfaces the chosen stack creates, and compare that count to the stated per-chamber maximum before committing the stack.
Prefer the narrowest stack -- fewest wafers -- that still admits every required cut in that chamber; widen only when a required key is otherwise excluded.

If the required set would force more interfaces than the cap allows, carry the distinction in a different chamber instead of adding a wafer: a lock rejects a key as soon as any one chamber excludes it, so rejection power can be moved freely between chambers while acceptance cannot.
Recheck the cap across every chamber of every lock as a pre-submit invariant, including the locks nobody flagged, because the same construction habit produces the same overshoot everywhere.
successSignals: No shear-limit violation is reported on any chamber of any lock.
Stack widths are chosen deliberately per chamber rather than by a uniform widening rule.
failureSignals: A check reports a chamber whose shear points exceed the maximum.
The over-cap chambers belong to the locks built to admit the most keys -- consistent with widening stacks to force acceptance.
The cap is only mentioned after the verifier reports it, never during construction.
recovery: When a chamber is over cap, rebuild that chamber's stack minimally and confirm that the required cuts are still admitted before moving to the next lock.
If the minimum stack still overshoots, redistribute the rejection across chambers rather than accepting the violation.
invariants: A chamber's shear points equal the number of interfaces in its stack; adding a wafer never reduces them.
The cap is per chamber, so a wide stack in one chamber is not offset by a narrow stack elsewhere.

proposals.title: Submit at the first clean check instead of spending the remaining actions on ghost counts
proposals.trigger: A check returns with no required failures and no forbidden openings, while the environment still shows remaining actions and a nonzero unlisted-ghost count that the task text explicitly calls an efficiency measure rather than a success constraint.
procedure: Submit immediately on a clean check. The assignment that reproduces the table is the deliverable; further checks cannot improve whether it is correct.
Treat the ghost count as a score tiebreaker only. Never spend a check, and never re-edit an assignment that already reproduces the table, in order to move it.
If actions remain and no clean check has been reached, spend them on a full re-derivation of the assignment, not on repeated confirmations of the same one.
Before each check, ask what you would change if it came back clean; if the answer is nothing that affects the access table, the check is not worth its cost.
successSignals: Exactly one check, followed directly by submission.
Submission with a large nonzero ghost count, still scored as a correct result.
Remaining actions left unused after a clean result.
failureSignals: Checks consume the entire action budget.
Submission occurs with remaining actions at or near zero and violations still open.
The same assignment is re-checked without a derived change between checks.
recovery: Once a clean check has been seen, the next action is submit -- not another check.
If a check is being used to decide what to edit, the edit should have been derived from the table without it.
invariants: The success condition is the access table alone; the unlisted-ghost count is not part of it.
Every check is an action that cannot be recovered, so a check is worth issuing only for a decision it changes.
